Name: subliminal_audit
Title: Fingerprinting Hidden Signals: A Gradient-Alignment Audit and Transformation-Robustness Study of Subliminal Learning
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal signals in seemingly-innocuous data leave a detectable gradient fingerprint that aligns with a small number of latent directions, enabling a lightweight pre-training data audit that flags subliminally-laden datasets without knowing the trait in advance; furthermore, we hypothesize that surface-form-preserving data transformations (numeric re-encoding, format paraphrase) selectively destroy the subliminal channel while preserving benign content, offering a cheap defense.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/2026) introduced subliminal learning and showed it requires matched base models. Blank et al. and Hadley & Gultepe show it is mediated by steering-vector distillation with gradients aligning to the teacher's steering direction; Nief et al. frame it as a LoRA/context artifact tied to shared template tokens; Aden-Ali et al. give a log-linear mechanism (LLS) for selecting subliminal subsets. Defenses so far are reactive: Narang et al. use inference-time consensus decoding, and prior work tries data filtering. What is missing is (1) a proactive, trait-agnostic data audit that detects whether a dataset carries ANY subliminal signal before training a student, and (2) a systematic characterization of which data transformations break the channel. We leverage the gradient-alignment insight not to explain but to build a practical detector, and we test transformation-based defenses that exploit the finding that the signal lives in non-semantic surface structure (specific tokens/format), distinguishing us clearly from mechanistic and reactive-defense papers.
Abstract: Subliminal learning lets a teacher language model transmit behavioral traits (e.g., a preference for owls, or misalignment) to a student via data that is semantically unrelated to the trait, such as number sequences. Recent work explains this as steering-vector distillation and shows that gradients on subliminal data align with the teacher's hidden steering direction. We turn this mechanistic observation into a practical, trait-agnostic tool. First, we propose a Subliminal Gradient Audit (SGA): given a candidate training dataset and a base model, we compute per-example activation-gradient statistics on the base model and test whether they concentrate along a low-dimensional subspace that is anomalously consistent across otherwise unrelated examples—a signature of an embedded steering vector. Because SGA never needs to know the target trait, it can flag poisoned datasets that pass keyword filtering. Second, we study transformation-robustness: we apply surface-form-preserving transformations (numeric base re-encoding, digit permutation, chat-template stripping, paraphrasing) and measure how much each destroys subliminal transfer versus benign task performance. We hypothesize a favorable trade-off exists because the channel lives in specific non-semantic surface tokens. We validate on the original owl/misalignment settings plus new traits across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma. Metrics: trait-transfer rate, AUROC of SGA detection at varying poison fractions, and benign-task retention. Deliverables are (i) the first proactive dataset auditor for subliminal signals and (ii) an evidence-based transformation defense, giving practitioners actionable pre-training safeguards for distillation pipelines.
Experiments: 1) Reproduce subliminal transfer: fine-tune students on teacher-generated number sequences with matched base models (Qwen2.5, Llama-3, Gemma-2) across 10 traits (animal preferences, tree preferences, color, plus misalignment) x multiple seeds; confirm transfer and no-transfer for mismatched bases as controls. 2) Subliminal Gradient Audit: for each training example, compute activation gradients (or per-example loss gradients projected to a low-rank random sketch) on the frozen base model; estimate the top principal direction across examples and a concentration score (ratio of leading singular value to bulk). Compare clean data vs subliminally-laden data. Report AUROC for detecting laden vs clean datasets as a function of poison fraction (1%,5%,20%,100%) and trait. Compare against baselines: n-gram/keyword filtering, embedding-anomaly detection, and perplexity filtering. 3) Cross-trait generalization of detector: does a threshold calibrated on one trait detect others? 4) Transformation-robustness defense: apply (a) numeric base re-encoding (base-10 to base-8/hex), (b) random digit permutation with consistent mapping, (c) chat-template/system-prompt stripping and re-templating, (d) LLM paraphrase of formatting, and (e) full-fine-tune vs LoRA. Measure residual trait-transfer rate and benign-task accuracy (GSM8K subset for reasoning traces, HumanEval subset for code) to quantify the safety/utility trade-off; produce Pareto curves. 5) Ablations: adaptive vs SGD optimizer, LoRA rank sweep, layer localization of the detected direction. Evaluation metrics: trait-transfer rate (LLM-judge probability of exhibiting trait), detection AUROC/F1, benign-task retention, and cosine similarity between SGA-recovered direction and known teacher steering vectors (where available).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) SGA may only detect steering-vector-style biases and miss subliminal signals encoded through other mechanisms, limiting its coverage. 2) Nief et al. suggest subliminal learning can be a fragile LoRA/context artifact; if transfer is weak under our settings, both detection AUROC and defense evaluation could be noisy—mitigated by using the strongest known transfer regimes and multiple seeds. 3) Gradient audits over large datasets are compute-heavy; we mitigate via random-projection sketches and subsampling but this may reduce sensitivity. 4) Transformation defenses that break the channel might also degrade benign performance (e.g., re-encoding numeric reasoning), so the trade-off may be unfavorable for some traits. 5) Results may be model-family specific; we address this with three base models but cannot guarantee frontier-scale generality.
